- Use `text-wrap: balance` on h1–h3 for even line lengths; `text-wrap: pretty` on long prose to reduce orphans.

#### Layout

- Vary spacing for rhythm.
- Cards are the lazy answer. Use them only when they're truly the best affordance. Nested cards are always wrong.
- Flexbox for 1D, Grid for 2D. Don't default to Grid when `flex-wrap` would be simpler.
- For responsive grids without breakpoints: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))`.
- Build a semantic z-index scale (dropdown → sticky → modal-backdrop → modal → toast → tooltip). Never arbitrary values like 999 or 9999.

#### Motion
- Motion should be intentional, and not be an afterthought. consider it as part of the build.
- Don't animate CSS layout properties unless truly needed.
- Ease out with exponential curves (ease-out-quart / quint / expo). No bounce, no elastic.
- Use libraries for more advanced motion needs (e.g. motion, gsap, anime.js, lenis etc)
- Reduced motion is not optional. Every animation needs a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` alternative: typically a crossfade or instant transition.
- Staggering the items within one list is legitimate. The tell is the uniform reflex (one identical entrance applied to every section), not motion itself; each reveal should fit what it reveals. Suppressing the reflex is never a reason to ship a page with no motion at all.
- Reveal animations must enhance an already-visible default. Don't gate content visibility on a class-triggered transition; transitions pause on hidden tabs and headless renderers, so the reveal never fires and the section ships blank.
- Premium motion materials are not just transform/opacity. Blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow/glow are part of the palette when they materially improve the effect and stay smooth.

#### Interaction

- Dropdowns rendered with `position: absolute` inside an `overflow: hidden` or `overflow: auto` container will be clipped. Use the native `<dialog>` / popover API, `position: fixed`, or a portal to escape the stacking context.

### New projects only (when no prior work exists)

#### Color & Theme

- Use OKLCH.
- **The cream / sand / beige body bg is the saturated AI default of 2026.** The whole warm-neutral band (OKLCH L 0.84-0.97, C < 0.06, hue 40-100) reads as cream/sand/paper/parchment regardless of what you call it. Token names like `--paper`, `--cream`, `--sand`, `--bone`, `--flour`, `--linen`, `--parchment`, `--wheat`, `--biscuit`, `--ivory` are tells in themselves. If the brief is "warm, traditional, family-coastal-Italian" or "magazine-warm" or "editorial-restraint", DO NOT translate that into a near-white warm-tinted bg; that's the AI move. Pick: (a) a saturated brand color as the body (terracotta, oxblood, deep ochre, near-black), (b) a true off-white at chroma 0 (or chroma toward the brand's own hue, not toward warmth-by-default), or (c) a darker mid-tone tinted neutral that's clearly the brand's own. "Warmth" in the brand is carried by accent + typography + imagery, not by body bg.
- Tinted neutrals: add 0.005–0.015 chroma toward the brand's hue. Don't default-tint toward warm or cool "because the brand feels that way"; that's the cross-project monoculture move.
- When picking a theme: Dark vs. light is never a default. Not dark "because tools look cool dark." Not light "to be safe.".Before choosing, write one sentence of physical scene: who uses this, where, under what ambient light, in what mood. If the sentence doesn't force the answer, it's not concrete enough. Add detail until it does.
- Pick a **color strategy** before picking colors. Four steps on the commitment axis:
  - **Restrained**: tinted neutrals + one accent ≤10%. Product default; brand minimalism.
  - **Committed**: one saturated color carries 30–60% of the surface. Brand default for identity-driven pages.
  - **Full palette**: 3–4 named roles, each used deliberately. Brand campaigns; product data viz.
  - **Drenched**: the surface IS the color. Brand heroes, campaign pages.

### Absolute bans

Match-and-refuse. If you're about to write any of these, rewrite the element with different structure.

- **Side-stripe borders.** `border-left` or `border-right` greater than 1px as a colored accent on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts. Never intentional. Rewrite with full borders, background tints, leading numbers/icons, or nothing.
- **Gradient text.** `background-clip: text` combined with a gradient background. Decorative, never meaningful. Use a single solid color. Emphasis via weight or size.
- **Glassmorphism as default.** Blurs and glass cards used decoratively. Rare and purposeful, or nothing.
- **The hero-metric template.** Big number, small label, supporting stats, gradient accent. SaaS cliché.
- **Identical card grids.** Same-sized cards with icon + heading + text, repeated endlessly.
- **Tiny uppercase tracked eyebrow above every section.** The 2023-era kicker (small all-caps text with wide tracking, "ABOUT" "PROCESS" "PRICING" above each heading) is now the saturated AI scaffold; it appears on 55-95% of generations regardless of brief, which is the definition of a tell. One named kicker as a deliberate brand system is voice; an eyebrow on every section is AI grammar. Choose a different cadence.
- **Numbered section markers as default scaffolding (01 / 02 / 03).** Putting `01 · About / 02 · Process / 03 · Pricing` above every section is the eyebrow trope one tier deeper: reach for it because "landing pages do this" and you're scaffolding by reflex. Numbers earn their place when the section actually IS a sequence (a real 3-step process, an ordered flow, a typed timeline) and the order carries information the reader needs. One deliberate numbered sequence on one page is voice; numbered eyebrows on every section across the site is AI grammar.
- **Text that overflows its container.** Long heading words plus large clamp scales plus narrow grids cause headline overflow on tablet/mobile. Test the heading copy at every breakpoint; if it overflows, reduce the clamp max or rewrite the copy. The viewport is part of the design.

### The AI slop test

If someone could look at this interface and say "AI made that" without doubt, it's failed. Cross-register failures are the absolute bans above. Register-specific failures live in each reference.

**Category-reflex check.** Run at two altitudes; the second one catches what the first one misses.

- **First-order:** if someone could guess the theme + palette from the category alone, it's the first training-data reflex. Rework the scene sentence and color strategy until the answer isn't obvious from the domain.
- **Second-order:** if someone could guess the aesthetic family from category-plus-anti-references ("AI workflow tool that's not SaaS-cream → editorial-typographic", "fintech that's not navy-and-gold → terminal-native dark mode"), it's the trap one tier deeper. The first reflex was avoided; the second wasn't. Rework until both answers are not obvious. The brand register's [reflex-reject aesthetic lanes](reference/brand.md) list catches the currently-saturated families.

## Register

Brand: run the font selection procedure in [brand.md](brand.md). Fluid `clamp()` scale, ≥1.25 ratio between steps.

Product: system fonts and familiar sans stacks are legitimate here. One well-tuned family typically carries the whole UI. Fixed `rem` scale, 1.125–1.2 ratio between more closely-spaced steps.

## Assess Current Typography

Analyze what's weak or generic about the current type:

1. **Font choices**:
   - Are we using invisible defaults? (Inter, Roboto, Arial, Open Sans, system defaults)
   - Does the font match the brand personality? (A playful brand shouldn't use a corporate typeface)
   - Are there too many font families? (More than 2-3 is almost always a mess)

2. **Hierarchy**:
   - Can you tell headings from body from captions at a glance?
   - Are font sizes too close together? (14px, 15px, 16px = muddy hierarchy)
   - Are weight contrasts strong enough? (Medium vs Regular is barely visible)

3. **Sizing & scale**:
   - Is there a consistent type scale, or are sizes arbitrary?
   - Does body text meet minimum readability? (16px+)
   - Is the sizing strategy appropriate for the context? (Fixed `rem` scales for app UIs; fluid `clamp()` for marketing/content page headings)

4. **Readability**:
   - Are line lengths comfortable? (45-75 characters ideal)
   - Is line-height appropriate for the font and context?
   - Is there enough contrast between text and background?

5. **Consistency**:
   - Are the same elements styled the same way throughout?
   - Are font weights used consistently? (Not bold in one section, semibold in another for the same role)
   - Is letter-spacing intentional or default everywhere?

**CRITICAL**: The goal isn't to make text "fancier." It's to make it clearer, more readable, and more intentional. Good typography is invisible; bad typography is distracting.

## Plan Typography Improvements

Consult the [Reference Material](#reference-material) section below for detailed guidance on scales, pairing, and loading strategies.

Create a systematic plan:

- **Font selection**: Do fonts need replacing? What fits the brand/context?
- **Type scale**: Establish a modular scale (e.g., 1.25 ratio) with clear hierarchy
- **Weight strategy**: Which weights serve which roles? (Regular for body, Semibold for labels, Bold for headings, or whatever fits)
- **Spacing**: Line-heights, letter-spacing, and margins between typographic elements

## Improve Typography Systematically

### Font Selection

If fonts need replacing:
- Choose fonts that reflect the brand personality
- Pair with genuine contrast (serif + sans, geometric + humanist), or use a single family in multiple weights
- Ensure web font loading doesn't cause layout shift (`font-display: swap`, metric-matched fallbacks)

### Establish Hierarchy

Build a clear type scale:
- **5 sizes cover most needs**: caption, secondary, body, subheading, heading
- **Use a consistent ratio** between levels (1.25, 1.333, or 1.5)
- **Combine dimensions**: Size + weight + color + space for strong hierarchy. Don't rely on size alone
- **App UIs**: Use a fixed `rem`-based type scale, optionally adjusted at 1-2 breakpoints. Fluid sizing undermines the spatial predictability that dense, container-based layouts need
- **Marketing / content pages**: Use fluid sizing via `clamp(min, preferred, max)` for headings and display text. Keep body text fixed

### Fix Readability

- Set `max-width` on text containers using `ch` units (`max-width: 65ch`)
- Adjust line-height per context: tighter for headings (1.1-1.2), looser for body (1.5-1.7)
- Increase line-height slightly for light-on-dark text
- Ensure body text is at least 16px / 1rem

### Refine Details

- Use `tabular-nums` for data tables and numbers that should align
- Apply proper `letter-spacing`: slightly open for small caps and uppercase, default or tight for large display text
- Use semantic token names (`--text-body`, `--text-heading`), not value names (`--font-16`)
- Set `font-kerning: normal` and consider OpenType features where appropriate

### Weight Consistency

- Define clear roles for each weight and stick to them
- Don't use more than 3-4 weights (Regular, Medium, Semibold, Bold is plenty)
- Load only the weights you actually use (each weight adds to page load)

**NEVER**:
- Use more than 2-3 font families
- Pick sizes arbitrarily; commit to a scale
- Set body text below 16px
- Use decorative/display fonts for body text
- Disable browser zoom (`user-scalable=no`)
- Use `px` for font sizes; use `rem` to respect user settings
- Default to Inter/Roboto/Open Sans when personality matters
- Pair fonts that are similar but not identical (two geometric sans-serifs)

## Verify Typography Improvements

- **Hierarchy**: Can you identify heading vs body vs caption instantly?
- **Readability**: Is body text comfortable to read in long passages?
- **Consistency**: Are same-role elements styled identically throughout?
- **Personality**: Does the typography reflect the brand?
- **Performance**: Are web fonts loading efficiently without layout shift?
- **Accessibility**: Does text meet WCAG contrast ratios? Is it zoomable to 200%?

When the type carries the hierarchy on its own, hand off to `/impeccable polish` for the final pass.

## Live-mode signature params

Each variant MUST declare a `scale` param controlling the hierarchy ratio. Express all font sizes in the variant's scoped CSS through `calc(var(--p-scale, 1) * <base>)` or, better, scale the type ramp via `clamp(min, calc(var(--p-scale, 1) * Npx), max)`. Users slide from subdued to commanding.

```json
{"id":"scale","kind":"range","min":0.85,"max":1.3,"step":0.05,"default":1,"label":"Scale"}
```

Where the variant riffs on a specific pairing, expose the pairing choice as a `steps` param (e.g. "serif display + sans body" vs. "mono display + sans body" vs. "all-sans"). Each branch routes through `:scope[data-p-pairing="X"]` selectors in scoped CSS.

See `reference/live.md` for the full params contract.

---

## Reference Material

The sections below were previously `typography.md` and live inline now so the typeset flow has its deep typography reference in one place. `bolder.md` also references this section.

### Typography

#### Classic Typography Principles

##### Vertical Rhythm

Your line-height should be the base unit for ALL vertical spacing. If body text has `line-height: 1.5` on `16px` type (= 24px), spacing values should be multiples of 24px. This creates subconscious harmony; text and space share a mathematical foundation.

##### Modular Scale & Hierarchy

The common mistake: too many font sizes that are too close together (14px, 15px, 16px, 18px...). This creates muddy hierarchy.

**Use fewer sizes with more contrast.** A 5-size system covers most needs:

| Role | Typical Ratio | Use Case |
|------|---------------|----------|
| xs | 0.75rem | Captions, legal |
| sm | 0.875rem | Secondary UI, metadata |
| base | 1rem | Body text |
| lg | 1.25-1.5rem | Subheadings, lead text |
| xl+ | 2-4rem | Headlines, hero text |

Popular ratios: 1.25 (major third), 1.333 (perfect fourth), 1.5 (perfect fifth). Pick one and commit.

##### Readability & Measure

Use `ch` units for character-based measure (`max-width: 65ch`). Line-height scales inversely with line length: narrow columns need tighter leading, wide columns need more.

**Non-obvious**: Light text on dark backgrounds needs compensation on three axes, not just one. Bump line-height by 0.05–0.1, add a touch of letter-spacing (0.01–0.02em), and optionally step the body weight up one notch (regular → medium). The perceived weight drops across all three; fix all three.

**Paragraph rhythm**: Pick either space between paragraphs OR first-line indentation. Never both. Digital usually wants space; editorial/long-form can justify indent-only.

#### Font Selection & Pairing

The tactical selection procedure and the reflex-reject list live in [reference/brand.md](brand.md) under **Font selection procedure** and **Reflex-reject list** (loaded for brand-register tasks). The rest of this section covers the adjacent knowledge: anti-reflex corrections, system font use, and pairing rules.

##### Anti-reflexes worth defending against

- A technical/utilitarian brief does NOT need a serif "for warmth." Most tech tools should look like tech tools.
- An editorial/premium brief does NOT need the same expressive serif everyone is using right now. Premium can be Swiss-modern, can be neo-grotesque, can be a literal monospace, can be a quiet humanist sans.
- A children's product does NOT need a rounded display font. Kids' books use real type.
- A "modern" brief does NOT need a geometric sans. The most modern thing you can do is not use the font everyone else is using.

**System fonts are underrated**: `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", system-ui` looks native, loads instantly, and is highly readable. Consider this for apps where performance > personality.

##### Pairing Principles

**The non-obvious truth**: You often don't need a second font. One well-chosen font family in multiple weights creates cleaner hierarchy than two competing typefaces. Only add a second font when you need genuine contrast (e.g., display headlines + body serif).

When pairing, contrast on multiple axes:
- Serif + Sans (structure contrast)
- Geometric + Humanist (personality contrast)
- Condensed display + Wide body (proportion contrast)

##### Web Font Loading

The layout shift problem: fonts load late, text reflows, and users see content jump. Here's the fix:

```css
/* 1. Use font-display: swap for visibility */
@font-face {
  font-family: 'CustomFont';
  src: url('font.woff2') format('woff2');
  font-display: swap;
}

/* 2. Match fallback metrics to minimize shift */
@font-face {
  font-family: 'CustomFont-Fallback';
  src: local('Arial');
  size-adjust: 105%;        /* Scale to match x-height */
  ascent-override: 90%;     /* Match ascender height */
  descent-override: 20%;    /* Match descender depth */
  line-gap-override: 10%;   /* Match line spacing */
}

body {
  font-family: 'CustomFont', 'CustomFont-Fallback', sans-serif;
}
```

Tools like [Fontaine](https://github.com/unjs/fontaine) calculate these overrides automatically.

**`swap` vs `optional`**: `swap` shows fallback text immediately and FOUT-swaps when the web font arrives. `optional` uses the fallback if the web font misses a small load budget (~100ms) and avoids the shift entirely. Pick `optional` when zero layout shift matters more than seeing the branded font on slow networks.

**Preload the critical weight only**: typically the regular-weight body font used above the fold. Preloading every weight costs more bandwidth than it saves.

**Variable fonts for 3+ weights or styles**: a single variable font file is usually smaller than three static weight files, gives fractional weight control, and pairs well with `font-optical-sizing: auto`. For 1–2 weights, static is fine.

#### Modern Web Typography

##### Fluid Type

Fluid typography via `clamp(min, preferred, max)` scales text smoothly with the viewport. The middle value (e.g., `5vw + 1rem`) controls scaling rate (higher vw = faster scaling). Add a rem offset so it doesn't collapse to 0 on small screens.

**Use fluid type for**: Headings and display text on marketing/content pages where text dominates the layout and needs to breathe across viewport sizes.

**Use fixed `rem` scales for**: App UIs, dashboards, and data-dense interfaces. No major app design system (Material, Polaris, Primer, Carbon) uses fluid type in product UI; fixed scales with optional breakpoint adjustments give the spatial predictability that container-based layouts need. Body text should also be fixed even on marketing pages, since the size difference across viewports is too small to warrant it.

**Bound your clamp()**: keep `max-size ≤ ~2.5 × min-size`. Wider ratios break the browser's zoom and reflow behaviour and make large viewports feel like the page is shouting.

**Scale container width and font-size together** so effective character measure stays in the 45–75ch band at every viewport. A heading that widens faster than its container drifts out of the comfortable measure at the top end.

##### OpenType Features

Most developers don't know these exist. Use them for polish:

```css
/* Proper fractions */
.recipe-amount { font-variant-numeric: diagonal-fractions; }

/* Small caps for abbreviations */
abbr { font-variant-caps: all-small-caps; }

/* Disable ligatures in code */
code { font-variant-ligatures: none; }

/* Enable kerning (usually on by default, but be explicit) */
body { font-kerning: normal; }
```

Check what features your font supports at [Wakamai Fondue](https://wakamaifondue.com/).

##### Rendering polish

```css
/* Variable fonts: pick the right optical-size master automatically */
body { font-optical-sizing: auto; }
```

**ALL-CAPS tracking**: capitals sit too close at default spacing. Add 5–12% letter-spacing (`letter-spacing: 0.05em` to `0.12em`) to short all-caps labels, eyebrows, and small headings. Real small caps (via `font-variant-caps`) need the same treatment, slightly gentler.

#### Typography System Architecture

Name tokens semantically (`--text-body`, `--text-heading`), not by value (`--font-size-16`). Include font stacks, size scale, weights, line-heights, and letter-spacing in your token system.

#### Accessibility Considerations

Beyond contrast ratios (which are well-documented), consider:

- **Never disable zoom**: `user-scalable=no` breaks accessibility. If your layout breaks at 200% zoom, fix the layout.
- **Use rem/em for font sizes**: This respects user browser settings. Never `px` for body text.
- **Minimum 16px body text**: Smaller than this strains eyes and fails WCAG on mobile.
- **Adequate touch targets**: Text links need padding or line-height that creates 44px+ tap targets.

---

**Avoid**: More than 2-3 font families per project. Skipping fallback font definitions. Ignoring font loading performance (FOUT/FOIT). Using decorative fonts for body text.

# Product register

When design SERVES the product: app UIs, admin dashboards, settings panels, data tables, tools, authenticated surfaces, anything where the user is in a task.

## The product slop test

Not "would someone say AI made this." Familiarity is often a feature here. The test is: would a user fluent in the category's best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?

Product UI's failure mode isn't flatness, it's strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.

## Typography

- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don't need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.
- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don't serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.
- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.
- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser; tables at 120ch+ are fine.

## Color

Product defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed (a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen), but Restrained is the floor.

- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.
- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only, not decoration.
- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).

## Layout

- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.

## Components

Every interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don't ship with half of these.

- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.
- Empty states that teach the interface, not "nothing here."
- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.

## Motion

- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow; don't make them wait for choreography.
- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal: nothing else.
- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don't want to watch it load.

## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)

- Decorative motion that doesn't convey state.
- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the "save" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.
- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.
- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).
- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.
- Modal as first thought. Modals are usually laziness. Exhaust inline / progressive alternatives first.

## Product permissions

Product can afford things brand surfaces can't.

- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).
- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.
- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.
- Consistency over surprise. The same visual vocabulary screen to screen is a virtue; delight is saved for moments, not pages.

# Product

## Register

product

## Users

Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.

Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.

The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.

## Product Purpose

A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.

The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.

Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.

## Brand Personality

**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**

- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.

Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.

## Anti-references

- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.

## Design Principles

1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.

Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.

# Design System: Email OS

## 1. Overview

**Creative North Star: "The Quiet Instrument"**

A precision tool used in long, focused sessions. The surface is a single warm charcoal plane. The interface recedes until only the list, the open conversation and the next decision are on screen. Density is high but calm: 36px rows, small type, no dividers, no cards. One violet signal marks where you are. Everything else is a tonal step on the same warm gray ramp.

The system follows Superhuman's browsing look closely, and that parity is an explicit goal. It covers geometry, density, type scale, tonal layering and the focused-row treatment. Features and workflows stay our own. The one place we deliberately go our own way is state: pending, failed, partial and outcome-unknown states are always visible in their own form (*"Honest state over smooth feel"*, PRODUCT.md). A quiet surface must never hide what happened.

The system rejects Gmail-web clutter, "AI magic" sparkle chrome, generic SaaS dashboards (card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels), and optimistic UI that says "Done" before the provider confirms.

**Key Characteristics:**
- Three fixed panes: a 40px icon rail, a fluid list or reader, and a 272px darker contact pane. Each is separated by a single 1px divider.
- One content inset (50px from the list pane's left edge). It aligns split tabs, sender names, date-group captions and banners.
- 36px rows on 12px type. Hierarchy comes from weight and tone, not size.
- Pane-edge alignment: the contact name sits on the split-tab line, and the contact email sits on the first-row line.
- Flat tonal layering. No shadows in the browsing shell.
- The violet accent appears once per screen: on the focused row or the active message.

**Layout geometry (approximate calibration targets).** These values come from the 2026-11-07 Superhuman reference capture (1603×2000 image px). The capture was scaled by about 1.56 image px per CSS px, calibrated from the macOS traffic-light pitch of 20pt and cross-checked against the 36px rhythm and the 40px and 270px pane widths in `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`. Verify them on real displays.
- **Rail:** 40px wide. The top action button (28px circle) sits on the split-tab line. The navigation icons sit in a 28px-wide dark pill below it, at a 28px pitch.
- **Split header:** 78px from the content top to the first row. Tabs are vertically centered about 42px down. The hamburger is centered 23px into the pane. Tabs start at the 50px content inset with an 18px gap; the count sits 4px after its label. Compose and search icons are right-aligned on the 32px action pitch.
- **Rows:** 36px. The highlight is inset 6px from both pane edges. There is a 44px left gutter, with the 5px unread dot centered about 34px into the row. The sender column is 132px, and subject→snippet→meta gaps are 12px. The trailing date sits about 25px from the pane edge. On focus, three 16px action glyphs replace the date at a 32px pitch.
- **Date groups:** a 48px block, with the caption vertically centered on the content inset.
- **Contact pane:** 272px with a 24px inner inset. The footer toolbar sits 24px from the bottom: a ghost label plus 16px glyphs at a 28px pitch.

### Parity Gaps (current code → target)

This is the backlog for layout, typeset and polish passes. Each gap names what ships today and what this spec requires.

1. **Split header.** Done (2026-11-07 header pass). The header is one borderless 78px strip inside the list column (the rail and contact pane span its height). It has a Graphite hamburger (Destinations navigator) centered 23px in, split tabs on the 50px inset (16px, active Paper White, inactive Smoke, 11px Ash count 4px after the label, 18px apart), and right-hand glyphs on the 32px pitch: Back (when there is history), Reminders (fixture only), the Starred-only toggle, Commands and Search. There is no brand text, no visible h1 while a tab is active, and no bordered chips. Glyphs are local inline SVG (`HeaderGlyph.vue`).
   - The context h1 stays in the accessibility tree. It is shown on screen, styled like an active tab, only when no rendered tab is active (Cached Done, Starred, Search, the reader, an open drawer).
   - The status line is removed. The inbox count is on the active tab; loaded counts were dropped as duplicates of the list. Selection count stays in SelectionBar, plus a visually hidden polite announcement. The pending count is covered by row "Pending…", the action notice and Activity. The Shift+U hint is in the Commands palette. The command error is its own alert line in the in-flow notice slot beside the action notice. The read-only hint and the Unread-only/Starred-only filter states stay visible in words in the header.
   - The Inbox coverage sentence is the tabs' accessible description and the tab strip's hover title. The browser-preview banner is a one-line amber "Preview · in-memory" note on the right; the full disclosure is its title and accessible text.
   - Utility drawers now start below the header, so they never cover its glyphs.
   Remaining: a compose glyph was deliberately not added, because there is no compose capability beyond local drafts in the Drafts drawer; decide whether "New local draft" earns a header slot. The aggregate pending count has no glanceable home outside Activity (candidate: an Activity rail badge in the rail pass). Calibrate the tab line against the rail's top button once the 40px rail ships (gap 2).
2. **Rail.** Today: a 5rem column of bordered text buttons (Inbox, Cached Done, Account, Activity, Drafts, Contact). Target: a 40px icon rail with a dark well group and 28px circular buttons. Labels move to `aria-label`/`title`. The repo has no icon set, so local inline SVG glyphs are needed (no CDN).
3. **Row metrics.** Today: inherited 16px text, `0.3rem 0.6rem` padding, `min-height: 36px`, a `border-bottom` divider on every row, sender `flex: 0 1 160px`, preview at 0.8rem. Target: 12px text throughout, a fixed 36px height, no dividers, 6px pane inset, 44px left gutter, 132px sender column, 12px gaps.
4. **Focused row.** Today: a full-bleed fill with a 3px inset bar. Target: a fill inset 6px from both pane edges and a 4px bar on the highlight's own left edge.
5. **Read state.** Today: a textual read-state label in the meta region. Target: a 5px `unread-marker` dot in the left gutter. Read state stays exact; when it is unknown, use a distinct hollow-dot treatment, never silence.
6. **Selection checkbox.** Today: always visible at the row start. Target: hidden until selection mode is active or the row is hovered or focused, and placed in the 44px gutter. While visible, the selected row keeps a non-color marker.
7. **Row actions.** Today: bordered text chips ("Mark read", "Archive", "More") that are always in the meta region. Target: icon-only `icon-muted` glyphs that replace the date on the focused or hovered row. Accessible names and the `meta-compact` overflow disclosure logic stay.
8. **Date-group caption.** Today: uppercase 0.72rem with letter-spacing and a bottom rule. Target: title case, 12px `text-secondary`, a 48px block, no rule, on the content inset.
9. **Contact pane.** Today: an uppercase "Focused conversation" caption, a 0.6rem pad, a semibold name, and a `minmax(230px, 280px)` width. Target: no caption; name in the 16px regular headline on the tab line; email in 12px semibold on the first-row line; a "Mail" section listing recent threads at a 24px pitch (this needs data the pane does not receive yet); a footer toolbar (a natural new home for Account, Activity and Drafts); 272px wide.
10. **Palette deltas.** `text-primary` changes from #ece9e2 to #ffffff, `text-secondary` from #a8a29a to #c0bcb6, and `divider` from #3b3936 to #474543 (pane separators only). New tokens: `text-tertiary`, `icon-muted`, `rail-well`, `rail-button`, `unread-marker`. `focus-accent` stays at the committed #bba5ed; the capture reads about #bfa1f6, which is within capture and color-profile noise.
11. **Global button style.** Today: every `<button>` is a raised bordered chip. Target: ghost buttons and glyphs in the browsing shell. Raised `button-utility` chips appear only inside utility drawers and recovery banners.
12. **Command overlay.** Today: hard-coded off-palette violets (#24212a, #17151d, #493d60, #c7a7ff, #81718f). Target: map them to `surface-raised`, `surface-contact`, `focus-fill` and `focus-accent`.
13. **In-flow bars.** The Selection bar, Action notice, cached-coverage note and draft-recovery banner use bordered full-width strips with mixed paddings. Target: borderless, 12px, aligned to the content inset, and still in flow and always visible.
14. **Typeface.** Superhuman ships a proprietary face. We stay on local `system-ui` (no remote fonts), so glyph widths will differ slightly. Calibrate sizes by eye on device, not by matching the font.
15. **Out of scope for this capture.** The native title strip (Tauri window chrome) and the reader view are not shown. The reader keeps its current tokens until a reader reference is captured.

## 2. Colors

One warm charcoal ramp, one violet signal, and two status hues reserved for truth-telling.

### Primary
- **Dusk Lavender** (`focus-accent`): the single "you are here" signal. Used for the 4px bar on the focused row, the active message bar in the reader, focus outlines, and the highlighted command. It never fills an area and never decorates.

### Secondary
- **Orchid Dot** (`unread-marker`): only for the 5px unread dot in the row gutter. It is pinker than Dusk Lavender so that unread and focus never read as the same signal.

### Neutral
- **Warm Charcoal** (`surface`): the list, rail and header plane. Everything sits on it.
- **Deep Umber** (`surface-contact`): the contact pane and utility drawers. It is one step darker, so context reads as secondary to the list.
- **Lifted Charcoal** (`surface-raised`): utility chips, overlays and inputs.
- **Focus Stone** (`focus-fill`): the focused-row and active-message fill, and the highlighted command item.
- **Inkwell** (`rail-well`): the pill behind the rail's navigation glyphs.
- **Rail Pebble** (`rail-button`): the circular rail action button.
- **Paper White** (`text-primary`): sender, subject, active tab, contact name and email, labels.
- **Ash** (`text-secondary`): snippet, date, group caption, contact threads, counts.
- **Smoke** (`text-tertiary`): inactive split tabs.
- **Graphite** (`icon-muted`): every resting glyph (row actions, compose, search, hamburger, footer icons, attachment). Hover and focus raise glyphs to Paper White.
- **Seam** (`divider`): the 1px vertical separators between rail, list and contact pane. Nothing else.

### Status
- **Amber Notice** (`warning`): pending, outcome unknown, local-only, expired-undo and partial states.
- **Coral Fault** (`danger`): confirmed failures and command errors.

### Named Rules
**The One Signal Rule.** Dusk Lavender appears at most once per screen, on the current row or message. If two violet things are visible, one of them is wrong.

**The Seams-Only Rule.** Dividers separate panes, never rows. Rows are separated by rhythm alone.

**The Status-Is-Sacred Rule.** Amber and coral are never used decoratively, and a status is never shown only as a tint: every status carries words.

## 3. Typography

**Body Font:** system-ui (with -apple-system, sans-serif)
**Label/Mono Font:** ui-monospace, for plain-text message bodies only

**Character:** One local system sans in two weights carries the whole UI. Hierarchy comes from weight (600 vs 400) and tone (Paper White vs Ash), not size. The browsing shell uses just two sizes.

### Hierarchy
- **Headline** (400, 1rem / 16px, 1.25): split tabs and the contact name. This is the only large text in the shell.
- **Title** (600, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): sender names, contact email, section labels ("Mail"), footer labels, notice labels.
- **Body** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): subject (Paper White), snippet and threads (Ash), date-group captions (Ash).
- **Label** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, tabular numerals): dates ("8:00 AM", "6 NOV" with an uppercase month) and counts in status text.
- **Count** (400, 0.6875rem / 11px): split-tab counts, set 4px after the tab label.
- **Mono** (400, 0.85rem, 1.45): the current plain-text message body in the reader.

Sizes are rem so the 16px and 20px root-font layouts in `tests/inbox-list.rendered-layout.test.ts` still scale. Row and header heights are min-heights in px. The 12px row size is measured from the capture: system-ui glyph metrics point to 11.5–12px.

### Named Rules
**The Two-Size Rule.** The browsing shell uses 16px and 12px only (11px for counts). A third size in the list needs a written reason.

**The No-Caps-Caption Rule.** No uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell. Date groups and pane headings are title case. Uppercase is allowed only for the month in compact dates.

## 4. Elevation

The browsing shell is flat. Depth comes from tonal layering: Warm Charcoal for the plane, Deep Umber for context, Focus Stone for the current row, Inkwell for the rail well. No shadows sit on rows, panes, the header or the rail. Shadows appear only on surfaces that truly float above the shell and cover it.

### Shadow Vocabulary
- **Drawer cast** (`box-shadow: -8px 0 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the right-edge utility drawer (Activity, Account, Drafts).
- **Popover lift** (`box-shadow: 0 6px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the compact row-actions disclosure panel.
- **Overlay lift** (`box-shadow: 0 16px 64px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.53)`): the command palette and navigator, over a `#00000088` backdrop.

### Named Rules
**The Flat-Shell Rule.** If something in the rail, header, list or contact pane casts a shadow, remove it. Shadows mean "this covers the shell", nothing else.

## 5. Components

### Conversation Row (signature)
The core of the product: dense, quiet and exact.
- **Shape:** square corners (0), a fixed 36px height, inset 6px from both pane edges.
- **Layout:** a 44px gutter (unread dot, or the checkbox in selection mode), then a 132px sender (Title, Paper White, ellipsis), then the subject (Body, Paper White) and snippet (Body, Ash) on one line with 12px gaps, then the trailing date (Label, Ash) about 25px from the pane edge. An attachment glyph (Graphite, 16px) sits before the date when present.
- **Focused:** Focus Stone fill plus a 4px Dusk Lavender bar on the fill's own left edge. The date gives way to three action glyphs (done, snooze, more) at a 32px pitch.
- **Hover:** a barely-there lift (`rgba(255,255,255,0.03)`). Action glyphs appear; focus and read state never change.
- **Pending / unknown:** an Amber Notice word ("Pending…") in the meta region, never just a tint.
- **Selected:** the visible checkbox plus a secondary inset bar, so selection never relies on color alone and never replaces the focus bar.

### Date Group Caption
- **Style:** Body, Ash, title case ("Yesterday"), on the 50px content inset, in a 48px block. No rule and no background band. Not focusable.

### Split Tabs (Navigation)
- **Style:** Headline type. The active tab is Paper White; inactive tabs are Smoke. The count (11px, Ash) follows 4px after the label and disappears at zero. Tabs are spaced 18px apart.
- **Header:** 78px tall, no bottom border. The hamburger is a Graphite glyph to the left of the inset; compose and search are Graphite glyphs on the right, at the row-action pitch.

### Rail
- **Style:** 40px wide on Warm Charcoal, with a 1px Seam on its right. The top action is a 28px Rail Pebble circle aligned to the tab line. The destination glyphs sit in a 28px Inkwell pill at a 28px pitch. The active destination glyph is Paper White and the rest are Graphite.
- **Labels:** icon-only on screen. Every button keeps its accessible name and `title`.

### Contact Pane
- **Style:** 272px on Deep Umber, with a 1px Seam on its left and a 24px inset. No caption heading.
- **Content:** the name in Headline on the tab line; the email in Title on the first-row line; a "Mail" section label (Title with a 16px glyph) followed by recent threads (Body, Ash, ellipsis, 24px pitch); exact known data only, never invented enrichment.
- **Footer:** pinned 24px from the bottom. A ghost Title label plus Graphite glyphs at a 28px pitch hold the utilities.

### Buttons
- **Ghost (browsing shell):** transparent, Paper White Title text or a Graphite glyph, 4px radius, `2px 8px`. On hover or focus, the glyph rises to Paper White; the focus ring is a 2px Dusk Lavender outline at a 1px offset.
- **Utility (drawers, recovery banners):** a Lifted Charcoal fill with a 1px Seam border, 4px radius, `2px 8px`. This is the only bordered button.

### Command Overlay
- **Style:** a Lifted Charcoal panel, 10px radius, 576px max width, Overlay lift, 15vh from the top. The input sits on Deep Umber with a 1px Dusk Lavender border. The highlighted item gets a Focus Stone fill plus a 3px Dusk Lavender left bar. Shortcuts are shown as `kbd` in Ash.

### Inputs / Fields
- **Style:** a Lifted Charcoal fill, a 1px Seam border, 4px radius, inherited font.
- **Focus:** the border shifts to Dusk Lavender. No glow.

### In-flow Notices (Action notice, Selection bar, coverage and recovery)
- **Style:** borderless strips in normal flow above the list, aligned to the 50px content inset, in Body type. Status words use Amber Notice or Coral Fault. Undo shows its `kbd` hint in Ash. They never overlay rows and never auto-hide a failure.

## 6. Do's and Don'ts

### Do:
- **Do** keep rows at exactly 36px with 12px type, and separate them by rhythm alone.
- **Do** align split tabs, sender names, date captions and notices to the single 50px content inset.
- **Do** use Dusk Lavender (#bba5ed) only for the current row or message, and the focus ring.
- **Do** show every pending, partial, failed and outcome-unknown state in words, in Amber Notice or Coral Fault, where the user is already looking.
- **Do** align the contact pane to the list: the name on the tab line, the email on the first-row line.
- **Do** ship glyphs as local inline SVG with an accessible name. No icon fonts and no CDN.
- **Do** treat Superhuman's browsing look as the visual and interaction reference. Close look parity is the goal (PRODUCT.md).

### Don't:
- **Don't** draw dividers between rows or under the header. Seams separate panes only.
- **Don't** use uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell.
- **Don't** add Gmail-web clutter: toolbars of rarely-used icons, or chrome competing with content.
- **Don't** add "AI magic" chrome: sparkle icons, or generated summaries presented as fact.
- **Don't** build a Superhuman feature-parity clone. Copy the browsing look, not Superhuman's product scope.
- **Don't** use generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics: card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration.
- **Don't** show optimistic UI that lies: no "Done" toast before the provider confirms, and no silent retry of an ambiguous send.
- **Don't** put shadows on anything in the rail, header, list or contact pane.
- **Don't** introduce a third type size in the list, or use off-palette hex values (the old command-overlay violets are the cautionary example).
- **Don't** load remote fonts, images or CDN assets.

## Validation and review ledger

Before integration, the parent independently ran all six `.pi/factory.json`
commands against untouched baseline application/test source: all exited 0. Core
reported 105 unit tests plus 7/8/30/15/16 integration tests, all passing. Default
UI reported 276 passed and 15 opt-in browser tests skipped (16 files). These
baseline results are not UX-03 validation. Logs: `/tmp/ux03-baseline/`.

The parent also reproduced the baseline default-locale Chrome row-layout result:
1 passed / 1 failed, exactly `Sep 30, 2001` versus `30 Sept 2001` at the existing
date assertion. The Vitest command exited 1; the diagnostic shell wrapper exited
0 because it printed the captured status. This is a failed gate, not a pass.

After integrating the backend handoff, parent `mise run test:core`,
`mise run check:contract`, and `mise run lint:core` all exited 0. Core now reports
184 passing tests (106 unit; 2 cached-Done; existing 7/8/30/15/16 integration).
The new temporary-SQLite tests cover archive→restart→query→restore, 137-result
bounds/tie ordering, failed/unknown/restored/new-arrival membership, foreign
accounts/cursors, and incomplete retained recovery after cache eviction/reopen.
Logs: `/tmp/ux03-integrated/`.

Initial combined parent checks: all six configured checks exited 0; UI 296 passed /
19 opt-in skipped. Parent Chrome discovery/reader/covered-focus suites: 17 passed.
A disposable external-copy negative control disabled the overlay propagation,
overlay-owner, and editable-target guards together: the real typing test failed
at its zero-mutation assertion, as intended. The actual checkout was unchanged.

The full en-GB layout gate caught a new rail-width regression (2 failures), which
was reproduced independently. The new Cached Done label widened the automatic
rail to ~139px, forcing More mode in previously inline scenarios. Bounding and
wrapping only that label restores both existing layout cases (2 passed); the
unrelated default-locale date limitation remains unchanged.

### Fresh review and accepted in-scope repairs

Two fresh-context read-only reviewers inspected actual integrated source/diffs.
  `pnpm exec vitest run tests/discovery.rendered.test.ts tests/reader.rendered.test.ts tests/disclosure-focus.rendered.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --minWorkers=1`:
  **18 passed** (5 discovery, 12 reader, 1 covered-focus). Each discovery case
  initializes fresh synthetic state. Both pointer and row-origin geometry paths
  pass; real input typing produces zero mutations; real Tab/Shift+Tab remain
  contained, and a highlighted lower result is revealed in a short palette.
- Existing layout suite under `LANG=C.UTF-8`: **1 passed / 1 failed**, exactly
  the unchanged `Sep 30, 2001` versus `30 Sept 2001` assertion. This default-locale
  gate remains failed, not green.
- The same existing layout suite with explicit
  `LANG=en_GB.UTF-8 LC_ALL=en_GB.UTF-8 LANGUAGE=en_GB`: **2 passed**.
- The earlier disposable-copy negative typing control failed at the intended
  zero-mutation assertion after all three typing guards were deliberately
  removed. This expected diagnostic failure does not alter the passing checkout.

The short-palette reveal addition also received a read-only scoped recheck:
**correct; no qualifying P0/P1/P2 findings**. Full visual/Superhuman fidelity is
not established by these synthetic runs.

Native fixture/WKWebView, OS-reserved key handling, IME, VoiceOver and native
restart recovery remain **pending**, not inferred from these checks. `pkg-config`
itself is unavailable in this VM; no prerequisite installation was attempted.

Application/test/core/native source hashes were recorded before the final browser
run and verified unchanged afterwards (excluding this documentation-only ledger).
At the end of implementation validation (before the operator's subsequent request
to open a PR), the index was empty and HEAD/origin/main remained `160d089`.
No staging, commit, push, PR, merge, deployment, mail access or publication had
occurred during implementation. The subsequent PR request authorizes branch,

content.text:
The typeset pass is finished on top of both earlier passes, and the uncommitted header pass is untouched. Typecheck is clean, `pnpm test` passes (639 passed, 32 skipped, up from 635 because of the new date tests) and every Chrome suite passes. Nothing is committed or pushed.

**Files changed:**
- `src/lib/browsing-dates.ts`: new fixed date format. Adds `fullDateLabel` and `machineDateTime`.
- `src/components/InboxList.vue`: the row date is now a `<time>` with a `datetime` value and the full date as its hover title.
- `src/components/ReaderView.vue`: both message timestamps show the full date and now have `datetime`.
- `src/assets/style.css`: type tokens, colour change, and every size in the shell mapped onto the scale.
- `src/components/AttachmentChooser.vue`: heading put on the scale.
- `src/components/RemindersPanel.vue`: `var(--border, #666)` was undefined; it now uses `--divider`.
- `tests/browsing-dates.test.ts`, `tests/inbox-list.rendered-layout.test.ts`, `DESIGN.md`.

**Type scale** (fixed rem, weights 400 and 600 only):

| Token | Size | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `--type-headline` | 1rem / 16px | Split tabs, context title, contact name, drawer headings; reader subject at 600 |
| `--type-body` | 0.75rem / 12px | Default for everything else in the main shell: rows, captions, rail, contact pane, notices, drawers, reader chrome, form fields. In-panel headings use it at 600 |
| `--type-count` | 0.6875rem / 11px | Split-tab counts |
| `--type-mono` | 0.85rem | Plain-text message body in the reader |

- Before, the shell used 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95 and 1.1rem plus text inherited at 16px. The only other sizes left are in the command overlay, which was out of scope.
- The contact pane caption is now sentence case, 12px, Ash, with no letter-spacing.
- The bundled detector no longer reports the flat-type-hierarchy or uppercase-caption findings. Only advisory colour/radius hits on overlay and shadow literals remain.

**Date rules.** Output depends only on the time, the current date and the viewer's time zone, never the browser locale. That follows the existing viewer-local time zone policy in the docs. Month group captions such as "October 2026" still follow the locale.

| Case | Shown | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Today | Time, 12-hour, no leading zero | "8:00 AM", "12:05 PM" |
| Earlier this calendar year | Day and month | "6 NOV" |
| Any other year, past or future | Day, month, four-digit year | "9 JAN 2025", "31 DEC 2025" when viewed on 1 Jan 2026 |
| Missing or unparsable | "Unknown" in the row, "Unknown date" in full form | |
| Reader and row hover title | Full date and time | "Thu 9 Jan 2025, 6:29 PM" |

- **Year form:** I kept the day ("9 JAN 2025") because dropping it ("JAN 2025") loses precision, and a two-digit year ("9 JAN 25") reads like another day number.
- **Uppercase:** the page text stays "6 Nov" and CSS uppercases it, so screen readers hear a word rather than letters.
- **Reader clock:** I used 12-hour instead of your 24-hour example so the reader matches the list.
- **Old locale issue:** the rendered-layout test that the docs recorded as failing outside an en-GB locale ("30 Sept 2001" vs "Sep 30, 2001") now passes under both en-GB and `C.UTF-8`.

**Colour changes and contrast.**
